assessmentSummary.identity: Traveling alternating straight-leg march at low speed with deliberate front-side leg extension, dorsiflexed presentation, controlled contact close to the hips, and no flight-driven bounding.
currentCardFindings: This directly duplicates Straight-Leg Bound March / Straight-Leg Run Prep when that card is interpreted as a march.
The two-repetition dose is ambiguous and should be passes or metres.
The card should not promise distance-jump performance; its observable purpose is learning a straight-leg contact pattern before higher-speed shuffle or bounds.

proposedDosage.progressWhen: the leg stays long without locking, contact remains close, and posture is stable

athleteInstructions: March forward with a long leg and place each foot close beneath you

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain one Straight-Leg March definition and consolidate this card with Straight-Leg Bound March. Remove 'bound' from the march identity; higher-speed shuffles and flight contacts belong in separate variants.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Straight-Leg Bound March addresses distance-jumping performance by targeting introduces front-side stiffness and pawback timing without the intensity of full straight-leg bounds. It should be coached with clear quality gates, honest phase placement, and enough recovery to preserve the intended adaptation.

evidence.sourceTitle: Jereem Richards’ games and drills to help develop speed
claims: World Athletics describes ankling as a progressive running drill that begins with learning a toe-to-ground loading action and then increases cadence.

Straight-Leg Bound March must state whether it is stationary or traveling, bilateral or alternating, walking, marching, dribbling, hopping, or bounding, its knee strategy, contact sequence, displacement, cadence, and terminal transition; spring or stiffness alone does not define identity.

evidence.sourceTitle: Women's 100 m — 2017 IAAF World Championships Biomechanical Report
claims: World Athletics treats straight-leg shuffle into sprinting as a drill progression that can be combined into a movement pattern congruent with the technical model.

Straight-Leg Bound March belongs to either low-amplitude cyclic plyometrics, sprint-mechanics locomotion, straight-leg shuffle or bound mechanics, or a compound transition; those categories must not be merged into one undifferentiated exercise.

evidence.sourceTitle: Ankle and Plantar Flexor Muscle-Tendon Unit Function in Sprinters: A Narrative Review
claims: The ankle and plantar-flexor muscle-tendon units make phase-specific contributions to sprinting, with distinct roles for soleus and gastrocnemius and important energy transfer at maximum velocity.

The card should identify intrinsic foot, plantar-flexor, tibialis-anterior, knee-extensor, hamstring, hip-flexor and extensor, lumbopelvic, and arm-action roles according to the actual drill rather than labeling every drill ankle-only.

evidence.sourceTitle: Kinematic Stride Characteristics of Maximal Sprint Running of Elite Sprinters – Verification of the Swing-Pull Technique
claims: Active foot contact with backswing velocity, small horizontal foot distance from the center of mass at contact, hip-extension velocity, and controlled support-leg flexion may help minimize braking during maximal sprinting.

Straight-Leg Bound March should cue contact close to the projected center of mass and observable rhythm without claiming that an isolated drill automatically reproduces or improves full-speed sprint mechanics.

evidence.sourceTitle: Application of Leg, Vertical, and Joint Stiffness in Running Performance: A Literature Overview
claims: Mechanical stiffness is task- and velocity-dependent, changes with fatigue, and represents coordinated whole-limb behavior rather than a fixed athlete trait.

Exercise difficulty must directly score technical complexity, physical and absolute-load demand, coordination, supervision, failure consequence, impact, work-capacity demand, and overall difficulty; audience labels are not part of exercise difficulty.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Plyometric Training on Lower Body Muscle Architecture, Tendon Structure, Stiffness and Physical Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
claims: Plyometric training can change tendon stiffness and performance, so low-amplitude contacts still require progressive exposure and contact-volume accounting.

Straight-Leg Bound March needs total and per-leg contacts, lane distance, surface, footwear, amplitude, cadence or velocity, approach and transition distance, technical-fatigue markers, between-attempt recovery, and weekly impact accounting.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Plyometric and sprint drills require progressive preparation, safe surfaces and lanes, suitable footwear, spacing, recovery, and supervision matched to intensity and complexity.

The card should require a level, dry, non-slip lane with a deceleration zone when traveling; a secured ladder only for the ladder variant; and an athlete who can tolerate the selected contact amplitude without pain or compensatory mechanics.

evidence.sourceTitle: Jereem Richards’ games and drills to help develop speed
claims: World Athletics gives an example of two passes over 10 to 20 metres for ankling and related running drills, while instructing athletes to learn the movement before increasing pace.

Use passes, metres, seconds, and explicit contacts rather than ambiguous repetitions; low-skill learning passes may use walk-back recovery, while bounds and bound-to-sprint transitions need fuller recovery and immediate quality stops.

evidence.sourceTitle: Kinematic Stride Characteristics of Maximal Sprint Running of Elite Sprinters – Verification of the Swing-Pull Technique
claims: Sprint-contact instruction should prioritize observable contact placement, active downward and backward foot velocity, posture, and rhythm rather than an unsupported promise of ideal technique.

Use a small task-specific cue set: stay stacked, keep steps short for ankling, contact close to the hips, preserve dorsiflexion without forcing a forefoot strike, let the heel behave naturally, and transition without reaching or locking the knee.

evidence.sourceTitle: Ankle and Plantar Flexor Muscle-Tendon Unit Function in Sprinters: A Narrative Review
claims: Sprint plantar-flexor demand changes across start, acceleration, and maximum-velocity phases and should not be represented as uniformly low load.

Stop for foot, shin, calf, Achilles, hamstring, knee, hip, or back pain; loss of balance; repeated reaching or hard heel strike; locked-knee braking; loud or lengthening contacts; cadence drop; asymmetry; ladder displacement; or an unsafe sprint transition.

evidence.sourceTitle: Women's 100 m — 2017 IAAF World Championships Biomechanical Report
claims: Sprint drills can progress from simpler to more complex tasks and combine into a sprint transition when the movement time and pattern fit the intended technical model.

Straight-Leg Bound March belongs after temperature and tissue preparation and before high-speed sprinting or high-output jumping; use learning versions in a mechanics block and bound or sprint-transition versions in a fresh output block.

evidence.sourceTitle: Jereem Richards’ games and drills to help develop speed
claims: Athlete support should show the exact movement at learning and performance cadence, the lane, contact sound, heel behavior, arm action, finish, and how a successful pass differs from merely moving the feet quickly.
Explain that stiffness means controlled resistance to collapse, not locking the knees or forcing the ankle, and show a lower-amplitude or slower-cadence option that preserves the identity.

evidence.sourceTitle: Application of Leg, Vertical, and Joint Stiffness in Running Performance: A Literature Overview
claims: Stiffness measures vary by task, speed, fatigue, maturity, and method, so coaches should not infer tendon or joint stiffness from appearance alone.

Provide side and rear observation, contact and distance counts, cadence or timing only when reliably measured, left-right comparison, surface and lane setup, phase placement, regression and progression rules, and a distinction between technical cueing and verified biomechanical measurement.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Exercise selection and progression should match readiness, technical competence, supervision, equipment scale, and the individual's physical and psychosocial context.

Accessibility options include shorter lanes, slower cadence, supported ankle loading, no-flight ankling, fewer contacts, visual floor marks instead of a raised ladder, quieter settings, extra demonstration, and longer recovery without converting audience context into an exercise-card classification.

evidence.sourceTitle: Women's 100 m — 2017 IAAF World Championships Biomechanical Report
claims: A straight-leg shuffle into sprint is a compound drill progression, not merely a renamed stationary ankle hop.

Cadence, pass length, contact cap, and coaching intent are delivery annotations; stationary versus traveling, bilateral versus alternating, flight versus no flight, straight-leg bound versus march, ladder constraint, and a terminal sprint may require a controlled variant or distinct definition.
